class="prose" id="body"><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s0"><p>Last week, we released <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows">dynamic workflows</a> in Claude Code. Claude can now write its own <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/glossary#agentic-harness">harness</a> on the fly, custom-built for the task at hand.</p>
<p>While the default Claude Code harness is built for coding, it is also useful for many other types of tasks because, as it turns out, many tasks resemble coding tasks. But there are certain classes of tasks where we have had to build custom harnesses on top of Claude Code to achieve peak performance such as <a href="https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11088861-using-research-on-claude">Research</a>, <a href="https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11932705-automated-security-reviews-in-claude-code">security analysis</a>, <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams">agent teams</a>, or <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review">Code Review</a>.</p>
<p>Workflows allow you to dynamically create harnesses built on top of Claude Code that enable Claude to solve all of those problems more natively. You can also share and reuse these workflows with others.</p>
<p>In this article, I’ll cover my initial workflows experiences and learnings so you can best take full advantage. Keep in mind, best practices are still developing: dynamic workflows often use more tokens and are best suited for complex, high value tasks.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s1"><h2 id="example-prompts">EXAMPLE PROMPTS</h2>
<p>Before diving into the technical details, I’d like to start with several example prompts to get you thinking about the possibilities with workflows:</p>
<p>&quot;This test fails maybe 1 in 50 runs. Set up a workflow to reproduce it. Form competing theories about the race, and don&#x27;t stop until one theory survives the evidence.&quot;</p>
<p>&quot;Using a workflow, go through my last 50 sessions and mine them for corrections I keep making and turn the recurring ones into <code>CLAUDE.md</code> rules&quot;</p>
<p>“Use a workflow to dig through #incidents in Slack for the past six months and find recurring root causes where nobody has filed a ticket.&quot;</p>
<p>&quot;Take my business plan and run a workflow where different agents tear it apart from an investor&#x27;s, a customer&#x27;s, and a competitor&#x27;s perspective.&quot;</p>
<p>&quot;Here&#x27;s a folder of 80 resumes, use a workflow to rank them for the backend role and double-check the top ten. Interview me using the AskUserQuestion tool for a rubric.&quot;</p>
<p>&quot;I need a name for this CLI tool. Use a workflow to brainstorm a bunch of options and run a tournament to pick the top 3.&quot;</p>
<p>&quot;Use a workflow to rename our User model to Account everywhere.&quot;</p>
<p>“Go through my blog post draft and verify every technical claim against the codebase using a workflow, I don&#x27;t want to ship anything wrong.&quot;</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s2"><h2 id="how-dynamic-workflows-work">HOW DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS WORK</h2>
<p>Dynamic workflows execute a javascript file with a few special functions that help spawn and coordinate <a href="https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents">subagents</a>:</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/405c8b387ec2cc574e6d48edba5431e02e23e4fca7c31d51184fc9738eaef70b.png" alt="The agent(prompt, opts) function with its options annotated: prompt is the only required input, schema returns validated JSON, model picks opus, sonnet or haiku, isolation is worktree or remote, agentType selects a subagent. Below it, parallel() fans out and waits for all; pipeline() streams each item through every stage." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1760" height="1216" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1760 / 1216"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG A</b><span>The three building blocks of a workflow script: agent() spawns one subagent; parallel() and pipeline() compose many.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Dynamic workflows also include standard JavaScript functions like JSON, Math, and Array, to help process data.</p>
<p>It’s particularly useful to know that dynamic workflows can decide which models an agent uses and whether subagents are run in their own worktree, allowing Claude to choose the intelligence level and isolation needed.</p>
<p>If a workflow is interrupted, for example by user action or quitting the terminal, resuming the session will allow the workflow to pick up where it left off.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s3"><h2 id="why-dynamic-workflows">WHY DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS</h2>
<p>When you ask the default Claude Code harness to do a task, it needs to both plan and execute in the same context window. For many coding tasks, this is highly effective, but it can break down over long-running, massively parallel, highly structured and/or adversarial tasks.</p>
<p>This is because the longer Claude works on a complex task in a single context window, the more it becomes susceptible to a few specific failure modes:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Agentic laziness</strong> refers to when Claude stops before finishing a particularly complex, multi-part task and declares the job done after partial progress, for example addressing 35 of the 50 items in a security review.</li>
<li><strong>Self-preferential bias</strong> refers to Claude’s tendency to prefer its own results or findings, especially when asked to verify or judge them against a rubric.</li>
<li><strong>Goal drift</strong> refers to the gradual loss of fidelity to the original objective across many turns, especially after compaction. Each summarization step is lossy, and details like edge-case requirements or &quot;don&#x27;t do X&quot; constraints can get lost.</li>
</ul>
<p>Creating a workflow helps combat these by orchestrating separate Claude subagents with their own context windows and focused, isolated goals.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s4"><h2 id="dynamic-vs-static-workflows">DYNAMIC VS STATIC WORKFLOWS</h2>
<p>You may have previously created a static workflow using the Claude Agent SDK or <code>claude -p</code> to coordinate multiple instances of Claude Code together.</p>
<p>But because static workflows need to work for all edge cases, they are usually more generic. With <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-8">Claude Opus 4.8</a> and dynamic workflows, Claude is now intelligent enough to write a custom harness tailor-made for your use case.</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/fb7abff3846443de3b59b23208f0019bad6eb2555e5dd945594438ce4ee143c1.png" alt="The question “Should we migrate our checkout service to a new provider?” handled two ways. A static harness runs five web searches, fetches results, verifies and summarizes into a generic research report. A dynamic workflow reads the billing code, checks each feature against the new provider’s docs, prices it at real transaction volume, runs a devil’s advocate, and ends in a specific recommendation." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1999" height="915" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1999 / 915"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG B</b><span>A static harness runs the same steps for every question; a dynamic workflow is shaped to the one in front of it.</span></figcaption></figure>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s5"><h2 id="helpful-patterns-when-using-dynamic-workflows">HELPFUL PATTERNS WHEN USING DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS</h2>
<p>You can start using dynamic workflows just by asking Claude to make one, or by using the trigger word “<code>ultracode</code>” to ensure that Claude Code creates a workflow.</p>
<p>But building a mental model for how dynamic workflows work will help you understand when to use them and how you might nudge Claude via prompts.</p>
<p>There are a few common patterns that Claude might use and compose together when building workflows:</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/0a60d2d8c1dbddc23694ead5848908e1f2c9ef9e57ed0fbdbf53a0dc11e9ed16.png" alt="Six workflow patterns as small diagrams: classify-and-act, fanout-and-synthesize, adversarial verification, generate-and-filter, tournament, and loop until done." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1999" height="1112" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1999 / 1112"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG C</b><span>Six workflow patterns Claude composes from.</span></figcaption></figure>
<h3 id="classify-and-act">Classify-and-act</h3>
<p>Use a classifier agent to decide on the type of task, and then route to different agents or behavior based on the task. Or, use a classifier at the end to determine output.</p>
<h3 id="fan-out-and-synthesize">Fan-out-and-synthesize</h3>
<p>Split up a task into many smaller steps, run an agent on each step and then synthesize those results. This is particularly useful for when there are a large number of smaller steps, or when each step benefits from its own clean context window so they don&#x27;t interfere or cross-contaminate. The synthesize step is a barrier—it waits for all the fan-out agents, then merges their structured outputs into one result.</p>
<h3 id="adversarial-verification">Adversarial verification</h3>
<p>For each spawned agent, run a separate spawned agent to adversarially verify its output against a rubric or criteria.</p>
<h3 id="generate-and-filter">Generate-and-filter</h3>
<p>Generate a number of ideas on a topic and then filter them by a rubric or by verification, dedupe duplicates and return only the highest quality, tested ideas.</p>
<h3 id="tournament">Tournament</h3>
<p>Instead of dividing the work, have agents compete on it. Spawn N agents that each attempt the same task using different approaches. Prompts or models then judge the results in a pairwise fashion using a judging agent until you have a winner.</p>
<h3 id="loop-until-done">Loop until done</h3>
<p>For tasks with an unknown amount of work, loop spawning agents until a stop condition is met (no new findings, or no more errors in the logs) instead of a fixed number of passes.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s6"><h2 id="use-cases">USE CASES</h2>
<p>Think creatively of when and how to ask Claude Code to make dynamic workflows. I’ve found that workflows are sometimes even more useful for non-technical work.</p>
<h3 id="migrations-and-refactors">Migrations and refactors</h3>
<p><a href="https://bun.com/">Bun</a> was rewritten from Zig to Rust using workflows. You can read more about how that was done in <a href="https://x.com/jarredsumner/status/2060050578026189172">Jarred’s thread</a> or see how we run <a href="https://claude.com/blog/ai-code-migration">AI code migrations</a> across million-line codebases.</p>
<p>The key is to break down the task into a series of steps that need to be operated on for example callsites, failing tests, modules, etc. Spin off a subagent for every fix in a worktree to make the fix, then have another agent adversarially review, and merge them. Consider telling the agent not to use resource intensive commands so that you can maximally parallelize without running out of resources on your machine.</p>
<h3 id="deep-research">Deep research</h3>
<p>We published a deep research skill (<code>/deep-research</code>) inside Claude Code that uses dynamic workflows. Specifically, it fans-out web searches, fetches sources, adversarially verifies their claims, and synthesizes a cited report.</p>
<p>But you may do this sort of research for more than just web searches. For example, asking Claude to compile a status report from context in Slack or to research how a feature works by exploring a codebase in-depth.</p>
<h3 id="deep-verification">Deep verification</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/14981a07d95b7a4f10f6e995e34ea589c6a87836a753f3ffd70047363adb34dd.png" alt="A report flows into a claim extractor, which fans out to claim checkers 1 through N, each optionally followed by a source auditor, converging into a verified report." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1999" height="800" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1999 / 800"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG D</b><span>Deep verification: one checker agent per factual claim, with an optional source auditor behind each.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>On the other hand, if you have a report where you want to check and source every factual claim that it references you may want to generate a workflow which has one agent identify all of the factual claims and then spin off a subagent to check each one in-detail. You could also have a verification agent check the source subagent to make sure its source is high quality.</p>
<h3 id="sorting">Sorting</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/be7b8dc2e6f8a2791efb3c4589fa182f0c90b380bb56d8b41a1f18fc7cb04394.png" alt="1,000 items enter a bracket: round one pairs items with a fresh agent per comparison, winners meet in round two, a last comparison decides the final, and the output is a sorted list." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1999" height="708" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1999 / 708"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG E</b><span>A tournament sort: every comparison gets a fresh agent, so no single context has to hold all 1,000 items.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>You may have a list of items that you want to sort by some qualitative measurement that you believe that Claude Code is good at evaluating, for example: support tickets sorted by severity of the bug. But if you try to sort 1000+ rows in one prompt, quality degrades and it won&#x27;t fit in context. Instead run a tournament, a pipeline of pairwise-comparison agents (comparative judgment is more reliable than absolute scoring), or bucket-rank in parallel then merge. Each comparison is its own agent, so the deterministic loop holds the bracket and only the running order stays in context.</p>
<h3 id="memory-and-rule-adherence">Memory and rule adherence</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/fd6d2a8544c5541442fb2df1c24374ff8e2984274cc2bf796fe5e632bfcc400a.png" alt="A diff of +142 and −87 lines is checked against five rules, one verifier agent per rule. Two rules flag lines 42 and 90; the rest come back clean. A skeptic agent re-reads each flag to separate real violations from false positives, leaving confirmed violations only." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1999" height="786" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1999 / 786"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG F</b><span>Rule-by-rule review: one verifier per rule in a clean context, then a skeptic filters the flags.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>If you have a particular set of rules that you find Claude misses or struggles with, even when put into the <code>CLAUDE.mds</code>, create a workflow with a list of rules that must be checked by verifier agents—one verifier per rule. Creating a skeptic persona subagent to review the rules to make sure they are in line will help avoid too many false positives.</p>
<p>The reverse direction works too: mine your recent sessions and code review comments for corrections you keep making, cluster them with parallel agents, adversarially verify each candidate (would this rule have prevented a real mistake?), and then distill the survivors back into a <code>CLAUDE.md</code>.</p>
<h3 id="root-cause-investigation">Root-cause investigation</h3>
<p>Debugging works best when you come up with several independent hypotheses and test them, but if you’re only using one context window, Claude can run into self-preferential bias.</p>
<p>A workflow can structurally prevent this by spinning up agents to generate hypotheses from disjoint evidence. For example, separate agents for logs, files, and data. Each hypothesis can then face a panel of verifiers and refuters.</p>
<p>This isn&#x27;t just for code. Workflows can be used for sales (why did sales drop in March?), data engineering (why did this pipeline fail?), or any post-mortem exercise.</p>
<h3 id="triaging-at-scale">Triaging at scale</h3>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/ebf352766b6bb484729e8a8c08f9a72f918b19f78d02e998fe3384fcf3fd88e3.png" alt="An untrusted backlog of support tickets, bug reports and user feedback enters a quarantine zone with read-only tools, where reader agents classify each item, dedupe against what is already tracked, and emit a structured summary only. A trusted zone with high-privilege tools holds an actor agent that acts on summaries, attempting a fix and opening a PR if fixable, otherwise escalating to a human. /loop runs it continuously." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1999" height="730" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1999 / 730"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG G</b><span>Quarantine, then act: reader agents touch untrusted content with no privileges; the actor agent only ever sees their summaries.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Every team has a support queue, bug reports, or some other backlog that cannot be fully processed by humans.</p>
<p>A triage workflow classifies each item, dedupes against what&#x27;s already tracked, and takes action. This could mean attempting the fix or escalating to a human user.</p>
<p>A useful pattern for triage workflows is quarantine. This involves barring the agents that read untrusted public content from taking high-privilege actions, which are instead done by the agents in charge of acting on the information.</p>
<p>Pair triage workflows with /loop to have Claude do this continuously.</p>
<h3 id="exploration-and-taste">Exploration and taste</h3>
<p>Workflows can be useful when exploring different approaches to a solution, especially when it is taste based, like design or naming, and would benefit from a rubric.</p>
<p>Try asking Claude to explore a bunch of solutions, and give a review agent a rubric for what a good solution looks like. The task is complete when the review agent feels like it has met the criteria. Solutions can also be ordered or selected via a tournament based on the rubric.</p>
<h3 id="evals">Evals</h3>
<p>You can run lightweight evals for particular tasks by spinning off separate agents in a worktree and then spinning off comparison agents to compare and grade the specific outputs against a rubric. For example, evaluating and then refining a skill you’ve created against a particular criteria.</p>
<h3 id="model-and-intelligence-routing">Model and intelligence routing</h3>
<p>Create a classifier agent tuned to your tasks that decides which model to use. This can be helpful when your task will involve many tool calls and conducting research prior to execution can identify the best model for the job.</p>
<p>For example, the best model for the task “explain how the auth module works” depends on how many files in the auth module there are and the shape of the codebase. A classifier agent can do this research and then route to Sonnet or Opus based on the expected complexity of the task.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s7"><h2 id="when-not-to-use-dynamic-workflows">WHEN NOT TO USE DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS</h2>
<p>Workflows are new. While there are many use cases where it will create outsized results, they are not needed for every task and may end up using significantly more tokens.</p>
<p>It’s best to use workflows creatively to push Claude Code in ways that you haven’t previously. For regular coding tasks, try and ask yourself: does it really need more compute? For example, most traditional coding tasks do not need a panel of 5 reviewers.</p>
<p>The same judgment applies one level up, at the architecture layer: the <a href="https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them">multi-agent vs single agent</a> decision follows similar logic — parallelism and specialization have to earn their coordination cost.</p>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s8"><h2 id="tips-for-building-dynamic-workflows">TIPS FOR BUILDING DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS</h2>
<h3 id="prompting">Prompting</h3>
<p>Detailed prompting, using the specific techniques we described above, for dynamic workflows creates the best results.</p>
<p>Workflows are not just for large tasks. You can prompt the model to use a “quick workflow.” For example, you can create a quick adversarial review of an assumption.</p>
<h3 id="combine-with-goal-and-loop">Combine with <code>/goal</code> and <code>/loop</code></h3>
<p>When using workflows that can be repeated, for example triage, research, or verification, pair them with <code>/loop</code> to be run at regular intervals, and /goal to set a hard completion requirement.</p>
<h3 id="token-usage-budgets">Token usage budgets</h3>
<p>You can set explicit token usage budgets for dynamic workflows to limit how many tokens a task uses. You can prompt it with a budget like: “use 10k tokens,” which will set the cap.</p>
<h3 id="saving-and-sharing-dynamic-workflows">Saving and sharing dynamic workflows</h3>
<p>You can save workflows by pressing “s” in the workflow menu. You can check these into <code>~/.claude/workflows</code> or distribute them via a skill.</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/c8b4b65c4c43f1d01be880efd0851cdfc50e8bd9c8517a57d16a761ce7d0331a.png" alt="The Dynamic workflows panel in Claude Code listing three runs with agent counts, token totals and durations: review-changes (14 agents, 482k tokens, 6m 12s), find-flaky-tests (6 agents, still running) and deep-research (22 agents, 1.1M tokens, 11m 3s). Footer keys: select, enter view, s save, esc close." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1278" height="350" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1278 / 350"/><figcaption class="cap"><b>FIG H</b><span>The dynamic workflows panel — press s to save a run as a reusable workflow.</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>To share them via a skill, put your JavaScript workflow files in the skill folder and reference them in the <code>SKILL.md</code>. To allow for more flexibility, you may want to prompt Claude to think of the workflows in the skill as a template instead of a script that needs to be run verbatim.</p>
<figure class="art-fig"><img class="fg" src="/media/d3d1c7dcf59433f5178c509e7510aad3d26c33ab53bddd712a244c00b37e1047.png" alt="A skill folder at ~/.claude/skills/deep-verify/ containing SKILL.md, verify-claims.workflow.js and rubric.md, beside the SKILL.md contents, which reference ./verify-claims.workflow.js to check each claim with its own subagent." loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1999" height="1016" style="display:block;width:100%;aspect-ratio:1999 / 1016"/></figure>
</section><section class="art-section" data-reveal="" style="--reveal-delay:.1s" id="a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s9"><h2 id="a-new-starting-point-for-discovery">A NEW STARTING POINT FOR DISCOVERY</h2>
<p>Workflows are a helpful new way to extend Claude Code. I encourage you to think of them as a starting point to explore new ways to use Claude to help accomplish your tasks. There is still much to discover in how to use them best. Let me know what you find.</p>
<p><em>For principles on what belongs in a harness in the first place, see our three</em> <a href="https://claude.com/blog/harnessing-claudes-intelligence"><em>harness design patterns</em></a> <em>for building with Claude.</em></p>
<p><em>This article was written by Thariq Shihipar and Sid Bidasaria, members of technical staff at Anthropic working on Claude Code.</em></p></section></div></div><div class="more-sec"><div Claude can now write its own \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/glossary#agentic-harness\",\"children\":\"harness\"}],\" on the fly, custom-built for the task at hand.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"While the default Claude Code harness is built for coding, it is also useful for many other types of tasks because, as it turns out, many tasks resemble coding tasks. But there are certain classes of tasks where we have had to build custom harnesses on top of Claude Code to achieve peak performance such as \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11088861-using-research-on-claude\",\"children\":\"Research\"}],\", \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11932705-automated-security-reviews-in-claude-code\",\"children\":\"security analysis\"}],\", \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams\",\"children\":\"agent teams\"}],\", or \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review\",\"children\":\"Code Review\"}],\".\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Workflows allow you to dynamically create harnesses built on top of Claude Code that enable Claude to solve all of those problems more natively. You can also share and reuse these workflows with others.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"In this article, I’ll cover my initial workflows experiences and learnings so you can best take full advantage. Keep in mind, best practices are still developing: dynamic workflows often use more tokens and are best suited for complex, high value tasks.\"}],\"\\n\"]}],[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s1\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"example-prompts\",\"children\":[\"EXAMPLE PROMPTS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Before diving into the technical details, I’d like to start with several example prompts to get you thinking about the possibilities with workflows:\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"\\\"This test fails maybe 1 in 50 runs. Set up a workflow to reproduce it. Form competing theories about the race, and don't stop until one theory survives the evidence.\\\"\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\\"Using a workflow, go through my last 50 sessions and mine them for corrections I keep making and turn the recurring ones into \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"CLAUDE.md\"}],\" rules\\\"\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"“Use a workflow to dig through #incidents in Slack for the past six months and find recurring root causes where nobody has filed a ticket.\\\"\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"\\\"Take my business plan and run a workflow where different agents tear it apart from an investor's, a customer's, and a competitor's perspective.\\\"\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"\\\"Here's a folder of 80 resumes, use a workflow to rank them for the backend role and double-check the top ten. Interview me using the AskUserQuestion tool for a rubric.\\\"\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"\\\"I need a name for this CLI tool. Use a workflow to brainstorm a bunch of options and run a tournament to pick the top 3.\\\"\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"\\\"Use a workflow to rename our User model to Account everywhere.\\\"\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"“Go through my blog post draft and verify every technical claim against the codebase using a workflow, I don't want to ship anything wrong.\\\"\"}],\"\\n\"]}],[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s2\",\"children\":[\"$L2f\",\"\\n\",\"$L30\",\"\\n\",\"$L31\",\"\\n\",\"$L32\",\"\\n\",\"$L33\",\"\\n\",\"$L34\",\"\\n\"]}],\"$L35\",\"$L36\",\"$L37\",\"$L38\",\"$L39\",\"$L3a\",\"$L3b\"]\n2f:[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"how-dynamic-workflows-work\",\"children\":[\"HOW DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS WORK\"]}]\n30:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"Dynamic workflows execute a javascript file with a few special functions that help spawn and coordinate \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents\",\"children\":\"subagents\"}],\":\"]}]\n31:[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/405c8b387ec2cc574e6d48edba5431e02e23e4fca7c31d51184fc9738eaef70b.png\",\"alt\":\"The agent(prompt, opts) function with its options annotated: prompt is the only required input, schema returns validated JSON, model picks opus, sonnet or haiku, isolation is worktree or remote, agentType selects a subagent. Below it, parallel() fans out and waits for all; pipeline() streams each item through every stage.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1760,\"height\":1216,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1760 / 1216\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG A\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"The three building blocks of a workflow script: agent() spawns one subagent; parallel() and pipeline() compose many.\"}]]}]]}]\n32:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Dynamic workflows also include standard JavaScript functions like JSON, Math, and Array, to help process data.\"}]\n33:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"It’s particularly useful to know that dynamic workflows can decide which models an agent uses and whether subagents are run in their own worktree, allowing Claude to choose the intelligence level and isolation needed.\"}]\n34:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"If a workflow is interrupted, for example by user action or quitting the terminal, resuming the session will allow the workflow to pick up where it left off.\"}]\n35:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s3\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"why-dynamic-workflows\",\"children\":[\"WHY DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"When you ask the default Claude Code harness to do a task, it needs to both plan and execute in the same context window. For many coding tasks, this is highly effective, but it can break down over long-running, massively parallel, highly structured and/or adversarial tasks.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"This is because the longer Claude works on a complex task in a single context window, the more it becomes susceptible to a few specific failure modes:\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"ul\",null,{\"children\":[\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"strong\",null,{\"children\":\"Agentic laziness\"}],\" refers to when Claude stops before finishing a particularly complex, multi-part task and declares the job done after partial progress, for example addressing 35 of the 50 items in a security review.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"strong\",null,{\"children\":\"Self-preferential bias\"}],\" refers to Claude’s tendency to prefer its own results or findings, especially when asked to verify or judge them against a rubric.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"li\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"strong\",null,{\"children\":\"Goal drift\"}],\" refers to the gradual loss of fidelity to the original objective across many turns, especially after compaction. Each summarization step is lossy, and details like edge-case requirements or \\\"don't do X\\\" constraints can get lost.\"]}],\"\\n\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Creating a workflow helps combat these by orchestrating separate Claude subagents with their own context windows and focused, isolated goals.\"}],\"\\n\"]}]\n36:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s4\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"dynamic-vs-static-workflows\",\"children\":[\"DYNAMIC VS STATIC WORKFLOWS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"You may have previously created a static workflow using the Claude Agent SDK or \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"claude -p\"}],\" to coordinate multiple instances of Claude Code together.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"But because static workflows need to work for all edge cases, they are usually more generic. With \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-8\",\"children\":\"Claude Opus 4.8\"}],\" and dynamic workflows, Claude is now intelligent enough to write a custom harness tailor-made for your use case.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/fb7abff3846443de3b59b23208f0019bad6eb2555e5dd945594438ce4ee143c1.png\",\"alt\":\"The question “Should we migrate our checkout service to a new provider?” handled two ways. A static harness runs five web searches, fetches results, verifies and summarizes into a generic research report. A dynamic workflow reads the billing code, checks each feature against the new provider’s docs, prices it at real transaction volume, runs a devil’s advocate, and ends in a specific recommendation.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1999,\"height\":915,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1999 / 915\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG B\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"A static harness runs the same steps for every question; a dynamic workflow is shaped to the one in front of it.\"}]]}]]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n37:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s5\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"helpful-patterns-when-using-dynamic-workflows\",\"children\":[\"HELPFUL PATTERNS WHEN USING DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"You can start using dynamic workflows just by asking Claude to make one, or by using the trigger word “\",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"ultracode\"}],\"” to ensure that Claude Code creates a workflow.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"But building a mental model for how dynamic workflows work will help you understand when to use them and how you might nudge Claude via prompts.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"There are a few common patterns that Claude might use and compose together when building workflows:\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/0a60d2d8c1dbddc23694ead5848908e1f2c9ef9e57ed0fbdbf53a0dc11e9ed16.png\",\"alt\":\"Six workflow patterns as small diagrams: classify-and-act, fanout-and-synthesize, adversarial verification, generate-and-filter, tournament, and loop until done.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1999,\"height\":1112,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1999 / 1112\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG C\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"Six workflow patterns Claude composes from.\"}]]}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"classify-and-act\",\"children\":\"Classify-and-act\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Use a classifier agent to decide on the type of task, and then route to different agents or behavior based on the task. Or, use a classifier at the end to determine output.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"fan-out-and-synthesize\",\"children\":\"Fan-out-and-synthesize\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Split up a task into many smaller steps, run an agent on each step and then synthesize those results. This is particularly useful for when there are a large number of smaller steps, or when each step benefits from its own clean context window so they don't interfere or cross-contaminate. The synthesize step is a barrier—it waits for all the fan-out agents, then merges their structured outputs into one result.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"adversarial-verification\",\"children\":\"Adversarial verification\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"For each spawned agent, run a separate spawned agent to adversarially verify its output against a rubric or criteria.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"generate-and-filter\",\"children\":\"Generate-and-filter\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Generate a number of ideas on a topic and then filter them by a rubric or by verification, dedupe duplicates and return only the highest quality, tested ideas.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"tournament\",\"children\":\"Tournament\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Instead of dividing the work, have agents compete on it. Spawn N agents that each attempt the same task using different approaches. Prompts or models then judge the results in a pairwise fashion using a judging agent until you have a winner.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"loop-until-done\",\"children\":\"Loop until done\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"For tasks with an unknown amount of work, loop spawning agents until a stop condition is met (no new findings, or no more errors in the logs) instead of a fixed number of passes.\"}],\"\\n\"]}]\n38:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s6\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"use-cases\",\"children\":[\"USE CASES\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Think creatively of when and how to ask Claude Code to make dynamic workflows. I’ve found that workflows are sometimes even more useful for non-technical work.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"migrations-and-refactors\",\"children\":\"Migrations and refactors\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://bun.com/\",\"children\":\"Bun\"}],\" was rewritten from Zig to Rust using workflows. You can read more about how that was done in \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://x.com/jarredsumner/status/2060050578026189172\",\"children\":\"Jarred’s thread\"}],\" or see how we run \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://claude.com/blog/ai-code-migration\",\"children\":\"AI code migrations\"}],\" across million-line codebases.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"The key is to break down the task into a series of steps that need to be operated on for example callsites, failing tests, modules, etc. Spin off a subagent for every fix in a worktree to make the fix, then have another agent adversarially review, and merge them. Consider telling the agent not to use resource intensive commands so that you can maximally parallelize without running out of resources on your machine.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"deep-research\",\"children\":\"Deep research\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"We published a deep research skill (\",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"/deep-research\"}],\") inside Claude Code that uses dynamic workflows. Specifically, it fans-out web searches, fetches sources, adversarially verifies their claims, and synthesizes a cited report.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"But you may do this sort of research for more than just web searches. For example, asking Claude to compile a status report from context in Slack or to research how a feature works by exploring a codebase in-depth.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"deep-verification\",\"children\":\"Deep verification\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/14981a07d95b7a4f10f6e995e34ea589c6a87836a753f3ffd70047363adb34dd.png\",\"alt\":\"A report flows into a claim extractor, which fans out to claim checkers 1 through N, each optionally followed by a source auditor, converging into a verified report.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1999,\"height\":800,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1999 / 800\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG D\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"Deep verification: one checker agent per factual claim, with an optional source auditor behind each.\"}]]}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"On the other hand, if you have a report where you want to check and source every factual claim that it references you may want to generate a workflow which has one agent identify all of the factual claims and then spin off a subagent to check each one in-detail. You could also have a verification agent check the source subagent to make sure its source is high quality.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"sorting\",\"children\":\"Sorting\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/be7b8dc2e6f8a2791efb3c4589fa182f0c90b380bb56d8b41a1f18fc7cb04394.png\",\"alt\":\"1,000 items enter a bracket: round one pairs items with a fresh agent per comparison, winners meet in round two, a last comparison decides the final, and the output is a sorted list.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1999,\"height\":708,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1999 / 708\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[\"$L3c\",\"$undefined\",\"$L3d\"]}]]}],\"\\n\",\"$L3e\",\"\\n\",\"$L3f\",\"\\n\",\"$L40\",\"\\n\",\"$L41\",\"\\n\",\"$L42\",\"\\n\",\"$L43\",\"\\n\",\"$L44\",\"\\n\",\"$L45\",\"\\n\",\"$L46\",\"\\n\",\"$L47\",\"\\n\",\"$L48\",\"\\n\",\"$L49\",\"\\n\",\"$L4a\",\"\\n\",\"$L4b\",\"\\n\",\"$L4c\",\"\\n\",\"$L4d\",\"\\n\",\"$L4e\",\"\\n\",\"$L4f\",\"\\n\",\"$L50\",\"\\n\",\"$L51\",\"\\n\",\"$L52\",\"\\n\",\"$L53\",\"\\n\",\"$L54\",\"\\n\"]}]\n39:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s7\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"when-not-to-use-dynamic-workflows\",\"children\":[\"WHEN NOT TO USE DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Workflows are new. While there are many use cases where it will create outsized results, they are not needed for every task and may end up using significantly more tokens.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"It’s best to use workflows creatively to push Claude Code in ways that you haven’t previously. For regular coding tasks, try and ask yourself: does it really need more compute? For example, most traditional coding tasks do not need a panel of 5 reviewers.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"The same judgment applies one level up, at the architecture layer: the \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them\",\"children\":\"multi-agent vs single agent\"}],\" decision follows similar logic — parallelism and specialization have to earn their coordination cost.\"]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n3a:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s8\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"tips-for-building-dynamic-workflows\",\"children\":[\"TIPS FOR BUILDING DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"prompting\",\"children\":\"Prompting\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Detailed prompting, using the specific techniques we described above, for dynamic workflows creates the best results.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Workflows are not just for large tasks. You can prompt the model to use a “quick workflow.” For example, you can create a quick adversarial review of an assumption.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"combine-with-goal-and-loop\",\"children\":[\"Combine with \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"/goal\"}],\" and \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"/loop\"}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"When using workflows that can be repeated, for example triage, research, or verification, pair them with \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"/loop\"}],\" to be run at regular intervals, and /goal to set a hard completion requirement.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"token-usage-budgets\",\"children\":\"Token usage budgets\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"You can set explicit token usage budgets for dynamic workflows to limit how many tokens a task uses. You can prompt it with a budget like: “use 10k tokens,” which will set the cap.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"saving-and-sharing-dynamic-workflows\",\"children\":\"Saving and sharing dynamic workflows\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"You can save workflows by pressing “s” in the workflow menu. You can check these into \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"~/.claude/workflows\"}],\" or distribute them via a skill.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/c8b4b65c4c43f1d01be880efd0851cdfc50e8bd9c8517a57d16a761ce7d0331a.png\",\"alt\":\"The Dynamic workflows panel in Claude Code listing three runs with agent counts, token totals and durations: review-changes (14 agents, 482k tokens, 6m 12s), find-flaky-tests (6 agents, still running) and deep-research (22 agents, 1.1M tokens, 11m 3s). Footer keys: select, enter view, s save, esc close.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1278,\"height\":350,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1278 / 350\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG H\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"The dynamic workflows panel — press s to save a run as a reusable workflow.\"}]]}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"To share them via a skill, put your JavaScript workflow files in the skill folder and reference them in the \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"SKILL.md\"}],\". To allow for more flexibility, you may want to prompt Claude to think of the workflows in the skill as a template instead of a script that needs to be run verbatim.\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/d3d1c7dcf59433f5178c509e7510aad3d26c33ab53bddd712a244c00b37e1047.png\",\"alt\":\"A skill folder at ~/.claude/skills/deep-verify/ containing SKILL.md, verify-claims.workflow.js and rubric.md, beside the SKILL.md contents, which reference ./verify-claims.workflow.js to check each claim with its own subagent.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1999,\"height\":1016,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1999 / 1016\"}}],null]}],\"\\n\"]}]\n3b:[\"$\",\"section\",null,{\"className\":\"art-section\",\"data-reveal\":\"\",\"style\":\"$2d:0:props:style\",\"id\":\"a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code-s9\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"h2\",null,{\"id\":\"a-new-starting-point-for-discovery\",\"children\":[\"A NEW STARTING POINT FOR DISCOVERY\"]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Workflows are a helpful new way to extend Claude Code. I encourage you to think of them as a starting point to explore new ways to use Claude to help accomplish your tasks. There is still much to discover in how to use them best. Let me know what you find.\"}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[[\"$\",\"em\",null,{\"children\":\"For principles on what belongs in a harness in the first place, see our three\"}],\" \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://claude.com/blog/harnessing-claudes-intelligence\",\"children\":[\"$\",\"em\",null,{\"children\":\"harness design patterns\"}]}],\" \",[\"$\",\"em\",null,{\"children\":\"for building with Claude.\"}]]}],\"\\n\",[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"$\",\"em\",null,{\"children\":\"This article was written by Thariq Shihipar and Sid Bidasaria, members of technical staff at Anthropic working on Claude Code.\"}]}]]}]\n3c:[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG E\"}]\n3d:[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"A tournament sort: every comparison gets a fresh agent, so no single context has to hold all 1,000 items.\"}]\n3e:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"You may have a list of items that you want to sort by some qualitative measurement that you believe that Claude Code is good at evaluating, for example: support tickets sorted by severity of the bug. But if you try to sort 1000+ rows in one prompt, quality degrades and it won't fit in context. Instead run a tournament, a pipeline of pairwise-comparison agents (comparative judgment is more reliable than absolute scoring), or bucket-rank in parallel then merge. Each comparison is its own agent, so the deterministic loop holds the bracket and only the running order stays in context.\"}]\n3f:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"memory-and-rule-adherence\",\"children\":\"Memory and rule adherence\"}]\n40:[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/fd6d2a8544c5541442fb2df1c24374ff8e2984274cc2bf796fe5e632bfcc400a.png\",\"alt\":\"A diff of +142 and −87 lines is checked against five rules, one verifier agent per rule. Two rules flag lines 42 and 90; the rest come back clean. A skeptic agent re-reads each flag to separate real violations from false positives, leaving confirmed violations only.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1999,\"height\":786,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1999 / 786\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG F\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"Rule-by-rule review: one verifier per rule in a clean context, then a skeptic filters the flags.\"}]]}]]}]\n41:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"If you have a particular set of rules that you find Claude misses or struggles with, even when put into the \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"CLAUDE.mds\"}],\", create a workflow with a list of rules that must be checked by verifier agents—one verifier per rule. Creating a skeptic persona subagent to review the rules to make sure they are in line will help avoid too many false positives.\"]}]\n42:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"The reverse direction works too: mine your recent sessions and code review comments for corrections you keep making, cluster them with parallel agents, adversarially verify each candidate (would this rule have prevented a real mistake?), and then distill the survivors back into a \",[\"$\",\"code\",null,{\"children\":\"CLAUDE.md\"}],\".\"]}]\n43:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"root-cause-investigation\",\"children\":\"Root-cause investigation\"}]\n44:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Debugging works best when you come up with several independent hypotheses and test them, but if you’re only using one context window, Claude can run into self-preferential bias.\"}]\n45:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"A workflow can structurally prevent this by spinning up agents to generate hypotheses from disjoint evidence. For example, separate agents for logs, files, and data. Each hypothesis can then face a panel of verifiers and refuters.\"}]\n46:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"This isn't just for code. Workflows can be used for sales (why did sales drop in March?), data engineering (why did this pipeline fail?), or any post-mortem exercise.\"}]\n47:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"triaging-at-scale\",\"children\":\"Triaging at scale\"}]\n48:[\"$\",\"figure\",null,{\"className\":\"art-fig\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"img\",null,{\"className\":\"fg\",\"src\":\"/media/ebf352766b6bb484729e8a8c08f9a72f918b19f78d02e998fe3384fcf3fd88e3.png\",\"alt\":\"An untrusted backlog of support tickets, bug reports and user feedback enters a quarantine zone with read-only tools, where reader agents classify each item, dedupe against what is already tracked, and emit a structured summary only. A trusted zone with high-privilege tools holds an actor agent that acts on summaries, attempting a fix and opening a PR if fixable, otherwise escalating to a human. /loop runs it continuously.\",\"loading\":\"lazy\",\"decoding\":\"async\",\"width\":1999,\"height\":730,\"style\":{\"display\":\"block\",\"width\":\"100%\",\"aspectRatio\":\"1999 / 730\"}}],[\"$\",\"figcaption\",null,{\"className\":\"cap\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"b\",null,{\"children\":\"FIG G\"}],\"$undefined\",[\"$\",\"span\",null,{\"children\":\"Quarantine, then act: reader agents touch untrusted content with no privileges; the actor agent only ever sees their summaries.\"}]]}]]}]\n49:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Every team has a support queue, bug reports, or some other backlog that cannot be fully processed by humans.\"}]\n4a:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"A triage workflow classifies each item, dedupes against what's already tracked, and takes action. This could mean attempting the fix or escalating to a human user.\"}]\n4b:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"A useful pattern for triage workflows is quarantine. This involves barring the agents that read untrusted public content from taking high-privilege actions, which are instead done by the agents in charge of acting on the information.\"}]\n4c:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Pair triage workflows with /loop to have Claude do this continuously.\"}]\n4d:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"exploration-and-taste\",\"children\":\"Exploration and taste\"}]\n4e:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Workflows can be useful when exploring different approaches to a solution, especially when it is taste based, like design or naming, and would benefit from a rubric.\"}]\n4f:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Try asking Claude to explore a bunch of solutions, and give a review agent a rubric for what a good solution looks like. The task is complete when the review agent feels like it has met the criteria. Solutions can also be ordered or selected via a tournament based on the rubric.\"}]\n50:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"evals\",\"children\":\"Evals\"}]\n51:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"You can run lightweight evals for particular tasks by spinning off separate agents in a worktree and then spinning off comparison agents to compare and grade the specific outputs against a rubric. For example, evaluating and then refining a skill you’ve created against a particular criteria.\"}]\n52:[\"$\",\"h3\",null,{\"id\":\"model-and-intelligence-routing\",\"children\":\"Model and intelligence routing\"}]\n53:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Create a classifier agent tuned to your tasks that decides which model to use. This can be helpful when your task will involve many tool calls and conducting research prior to execution can identify the best model for the job.\"}]\n54:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"For example, the best model for the task “explain how the auth module works” depends on how many files in the auth module there are and the shape of the codebase. A classifier agent can do this research and then route to Sonnet or Opus based on the expected complexity of the task.\"}]\n1c:[[\"$\",\"meta\",\"0\",{\"charSet\":\"utf-8\"}],[\"$\",\"meta\",\"1\",{\"name\":\"viewport\",\"content\":\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\"}],[\"$\",\"meta\",\"2\",{\"name\":\"theme-color\",\"content\":\"#141413\",\"media\":\"(prefers-color-scheme: dark)\"}],[\"$\",\"meta\",\"3\",{\"name\":\"theme-color\",\"content\":\"#faf9f5\",\"media\":\"(prefers-color-scheme: light)\"}]]\n55:I[27201,[\"$2\",\"$3\"],\"IconMark\"]\n19:null\n1f:[[\"$\",\"title\",\"0\",{\"children\":\"A harness for every task: dynamic workflows in Claude Code / claude.dev Blog\"}],[\"$\",\"meta\",\"1\",{\"name\":\"description\",\"content\":\"Claude Code can now write and orchestrate its own multi-agent harness on the fly.
